facts.claim: "Ballad of 1892" is track 1 on Jeremy Pinnell's album Ties of Blood and Affection, released January 27, 2017 on SofaBurn Records.
Jeremy Pinnell is credited as the writer and composer of "Ballad of 1892", which runs 3:05.

Discogs credits for the album list Jeremy Pinnell (acoustic guitar, vocals, producer), Brad Myers (bass, electric guitar), Adam Nurre (drums, backing vocals, percussion), Bob Nave (Hammond organ) and Cameron Cochran (acoustic guitar, pedal steel, backing vocals, on track B4 only).
Mike Montgomery is credited as producer, recording engineer, mixer and mastering engineer on the album.
The album was recorded, mixed and mastered at Candyland Recording Studio in Dayton, KY.
Mike Montgomery, owner of Candyland, named Ties of Blood and Affection among the last records he made using a fully analog tape workflow.

Ties of Blood and Affection is Pinnell's sophomore album, following the 2015 debut OH/KY. The label bio says it finds him taking comfort in his own skin and reaching the redemption only hinted at in his earlier songs.
Press material describes the album's songs as chugging along in a spring-reverb sound from somewhere between 1955 and 1975, rooted in Pinnell's steady acoustic guitar.
Rolling Stone called the album a stellar collection that could earn Pinnell comparisons to Sturgill Simpson.
Pinnell grew up in Elsmere, Kentucky, and has been making country music since his 2014 debut OH/KY.

research.lineage: Pinnell's song sits in the traditional, outlaw-leaning honky-tonk country tradition of northern Kentucky and Cincinnati, with a Bakersfield and 1970s country sound that critics compare to Waylon Jennings, Johnny Cash and Buck Owens.

draft:
The preacher shows up in the second verse, and the narrator of **Ballad of 1892** has no patience for him. "The preacher wanna tell me that he knows about hell," Jeremy Pinnell sings from a prison cell, and the next lines make the case against him: no job, no home, and a man of God who "don't know what it's like to be all alone." That's the song's sore spot. The narrator isn't asking to be forgiven. The narrator is asking someone to admit they don't know what this feels like, and the defiance carries something rawer underneath it.

The first verse sets up how he got here, and it barely flinches. A house "full of hookers and wine," a lover in the back room "done committing a crime." Then comes the line that holds the whole thing: "Bad times ahead good times behind." It's a shrug and a sentence handed down at the same moment. The chorus keeps circling back to the person he can't stop worrying about. *My baby gets high, walking the line.* That phrase belongs to Johnny Cash, and Pinnell bends it. In Cash's song, walking the line is a vow of faithfulness. Here it sounds like balancing on an edge, and the narrator watches from behind bars and can't do a thing. Love and helplessness sit in the same three words, and neither one wins.

The arrangement takes all of this calmly, and that's the trick. An acoustic guitar strums a steady rhythm. A clean electric guitar plays a simple melodic line that stays put the whole way. Bass and drums keep a plain, unhurried beat at a moderate country-folk pace. Pinnell sings straight and clear, telling it like a story, with no harmonies to soften anything. Nobody in the band raises their voice about the crime or the cell, so the feeling has to come through the words.

This is the first track on *Ties of Blood and Affection*, Pinnell's second album. His label describes the record as the one where the Elsmere, Kentucky songwriter finally reaches the redemption his earlier songs only hinted at. Putting this song first makes sense. It starts at the bottom, before any redemption arrives. The album was made at Candyland Recording Studio in Dayton, Kentucky, with Mike Montgomery producing and engineering, and Montgomery has named it among the last records he made entirely on analog tape. Press for the album placed its sound somewhere between 1955 and 1975, and the song fits that window: honky-tonk storytelling with outlaw country's grudge against anyone who claims to know better.

The song keeps you in that cell with someone who would rather be judged than pitied, and the line it keeps coming back to isn't about his own trouble but about the person outside who's still getting high.
